body:
Historical development of Gujarati

Gujarati belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European language family. It developed from earlier western Indo-Aryan speech varieties through the Middle Indo-Aryan and Apabhramsha stages.

Early Gujarati and related Rajasthani varieties shared important linguistic features. Over time, regional pronunciation, vocabulary, literary conventions and patterns of usage contributed to the emergence of more clearly differentiated languages.

The history of Gujarati is commonly divided into Old Gujarati, Middle Gujarati and Modern Gujarati. The exact boundaries of these periods vary among scholars because linguistic changes occur gradually.

Old Gujarati

Old Gujarati developed through the transition from regional Apabhramsha varieties. Jain scholars contributed substantially to its early written and grammatical traditions.

Religious narratives, poetic compositions and grammatical works helped preserve evidence of the language during its formative period.

Middle Gujarati

Gujarati became an increasingly prominent language of devotional literature, narrative poetry and public cultural expression.

Narsinh Mehta contributed to the development of Gujarati devotional poetry. Later writers such as Akho and Premanand further expanded the expressive and literary resources of the language.

Modern Gujarati

The development of printing, modern education, prose writing, dictionaries, newspapers and literary institutions encouraged the standardisation of Gujarati.

Writers such as Narmad helped develop modern Gujarati literary expression. The development of a standard written form did not eliminate regional speech varieties, which continue to form an important part of Gujarat's linguistic heritage.

Acharya Hemachandra and Gujarati linguistic history

Acharya Hemachandra was a prominent Jain scholar, grammarian and intellectual of 12th-century Gujarat. His works provide important evidence of the linguistic transition from Sanskrit and Prakrit to later regional Indo-Aryan forms.

His Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana is a major grammatical work covering Sanskrit and Prakrit, including Apabhramsha.

His Deshinamamala records vernacular vocabulary that was not adequately explained solely through conventional Sanskrit derivation. It is valuable for understanding regional linguistic traditions and historical vocabulary.

The Apabhramsha examples preserved in Hemachandra's grammatical work provide evidence relevant to the early development of Gujarati and related western Indo-Aryan varieties.

Panini is associated with the Ashtadhyayi and Sanskrit grammar. Hemachandra is associated with Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana and the grammatical traditions of Sanskrit, Prakrit and Apabhramsha.

The Gujarati writing system

The modern Gujarati script belongs to the Brahmi-derived family and is closely related to the Nagari writing tradition.

Its characteristic visual feature is the absence of the continuous upper headline found in Devanagari. Gujarati writing proceeds from left to right and employs vowel marks, consonant forms and combinations of consonants.

The evolution of Gujarati writing was influenced by manuscript traditions and practical uses such as commercial correspondence and account-keeping. Gujarati traders and merchants contributed to the widespread use of the script.

Regional linguistic diversity in Gujarat

Gujarati is the principal language of Gujarat, but the state contains numerous regional languages and speech varieties.

Language or speech varietyMajor regional association
KathiawadiSaurashtra
SuratiSurat and southern Gujarat
CharotariCharotar region of central Gujarat
KachchhiKutch
Bhili and related varietiesTribal regions of eastern Gujarat

Kathiawadi, Surati and Charotari are commonly recognised as regional varieties of Gujarati.

Kachchhi is a related Indo-Aryan language variety with close historical links to Sindhi and Gujarati. In Census 2011, Kachchhi was grouped under Sindhi rather than Gujarati.

Bhili and related varieties belong to the Indo-Aryan branch. Bhili/Bhilodi is separately listed among the non-Scheduled languages in the Census classification.

The Census grouping of a mother tongue reflects an administrative and linguistic classification used for statistical presentation. It does not necessarily resolve every question about community identity or linguistic independence.

Girnar inscriptions and the historical language heritage of Gujarat

The inscriptions at Girnar near Junagadh provide important evidence of language use during different historical periods.

The same large rock carries inscriptions associated with Ashoka, Rudradaman I and Skandagupta. Their inscriptions demonstrate changes in the literary language used for public records across several centuries.

RulerPeriodLanguage
Ashoka3rd century BCEPrakrit
Rudradaman IApproximately 150 CESanskrit
Skandagupta5th century CESanskrit

The inscriptions belong to different historical forms of the Brahmi writing tradition. Rudradaman's inscription is particularly important as an early extensive royal inscription in Sanskrit.

These records illustrate how a writing tradition can continue and evolve even while the language employed in public inscriptions changes.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarati developed through earlier western Indo-Aryan and Apabhramsha varieties.
  • Hemachandra: Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana and Deshinamamala.
  • Gujarati script lacks the characteristic Devanagari headline.
  • Kachchhi was classified under Sindhi in Census 2011.
  • Girnar: Ashoka's Prakrit inscriptions and the later Sanskrit inscriptions of Rudradaman and Skandagupta.
  • Trap: Not every language spoken in Gujarat is a dialect of Gujarati.

[Sources: GCERT, Class 10, Social Science, Gujarati-medium edition, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, pp. 30–33; Census of India, The Written Languages of the World: A Survey of the Degree and Modes of Use, Constitutional Languages, India, Gujarati section, p. 123; Census of India 2011, Table C-16, Population by Mother Tongue, Gujarat; Unicode Standard, Version 17.0, Section 12.4; Hemacandra, Siddha-Hemacandra-Shabdanushasana, Chapter 8, and catalogue of Hemacandra's published works; National Museum, New Delhi, Edict of Ashoka, Girnar; Significant Discoveries around Sudarshan Lake, Junagadh, IGNCA digital archaeological collection. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Gujarati Language, Script and Linguistic Heritage

body:
Why languages change

Language changes because communities continually adapt their communication to changing social and cultural circumstances. New words emerge, older pronunciations change, grammatical patterns develop and speakers adopt expressions from neighbouring languages.

These changes usually occur gradually. They may eventually produce distinctive dialects or new languages, especially when communities become geographically or socially separated.

Sound change

The pronunciation of inherited words can change over successive generations. Related languages may retain similar meanings while developing different spoken forms.

For example, the Sanskrit word dharma corresponds to the Prakrit form dhamma found in Ashokan usage. Such differences help illustrate historical sound change within Indo-Aryan.

Vocabulary borrowing

When linguistic communities interact, speakers may adopt words from other languages. This process is called lexical borrowing.

Indian languages have borrowed words from Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Portuguese, English and numerous regional languages at different historical periods.

Words such as darwaza and bazaar reflect Persian influence on Indian vocabulary. Modern Gujarati and Hindi also commonly incorporate English words relating to technology, education, administration and transport.

Tatsama and Tadbhava

Indian linguistic traditions distinguish between different historical sources of vocabulary.

  • Tatsama: Words adopted from Sanskrit while substantially retaining their Sanskrit form. For example, agni, meaning fire.
  • Tadbhava: Words historically inherited from earlier Indo-Aryan forms through successive linguistic changes. For example, Hindi aag, historically related to Sanskrit agni.
  • Deshi or Deshaj: Indigenous or regional vocabulary not readily explained as a direct Sanskrit borrowing or through the conventional Sanskrit-derived categories.

Tatsama and Tadbhava describe different historical relationships between words. They are not classifications of entire languages.

Standardisation and literary development

Printing, education, dictionaries, grammar books and administrative use can encourage the selection and spread of a standard written variety of a language.

Standardisation makes communication across different regions easier. However, it does not mean that every speaker must abandon a regional dialect or adopt identical pronunciation.

The emergence of standard Gujarati illustrates how a common written tradition can coexist with the linguistic diversity of Saurashtra, Kutch, central Gujarat and southern Gujarat.

Bilingualism and multilingualism

Bilingualism refers to the ability or practice of using 2 languages. Multilingualism refers to the use of multiple languages by an individual, community or society.

A multilingual individual may use different languages for different purposes, such as family communication, education, administration, business and interaction with people from other regions.

A multilingual society is one in which several languages are used, even if not every member of that society can speak all of them.

A resident of Gujarat may speak Kachchhi at home, use Gujarati in local commerce, communicate in Hindi with visitors and study technical subjects in English. The languages serve different functions within the same person's daily life.

Census of India 2011 records mother tongues in Table C-16. Table C-17 records bilingualism and trilingualism, including information on additional languages spoken by people from different mother-tongue communities.

Language shift and preservation

Language shift occurs when a community gradually begins to use another language in place of its traditional language across important areas of daily life.

Migration, education, economic opportunity and the social status of a dominant language may contribute to language shift. The acquisition of a second language, however, does not automatically result in the abandonment of the first language.

A language becomes endangered when it is no longer being transmitted reliably to younger generations and its community of regular speakers declines.

Documentation, dictionaries, oral-history recordings, publication, education and intergenerational transmission can help preserve linguistic heritage.

A language without an established script can still possess complex grammar, rich oral literature and extensive cultural knowledge. Preservation of linguistic diversity therefore includes spoken traditions as well as written texts.

Institutional support for Indian languages

The Central Institute of Indian Languages, established in 1969 at Mysuru, contributes to research, documentation, teaching and development of Indian languages.

Sahitya Akademi promotes Indian literary traditions, including literary publication, translation and interaction across language communities.

The Census Language Division collects and classifies linguistic information, providing a statistical basis for understanding India's multilingual population.

Prelims focus

  • Tatsama: Sanskrit-derived borrowing retaining substantially the Sanskrit form.
  • Tadbhava: historically inherited and linguistically transformed word.
  • Lexical borrowing does not change the genealogical family of a language.
  • Census Table C-16 concerns mother tongues; Table C-17 concerns bilingualism and trilingualism.
  • Language shift differs from the mere acquisition of an additional language.
  • Trap: An unwritten language is not necessarily linguistically or culturally less developed.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 8, p. 79; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 9, pp. 130–132; GCERT, Class 10, Social Science, Gujarati-medium edition, Chapter 4, pp. 30–33; Census of India 2011, Tables C-16 and C-17; UNESCO, State of the Education Report for India 2025: The Mother Tongue and Multilingual Education; Central Institute of Indian Languages, institutional and linguistic resource publications. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]
